📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fox News Digital spoke to Theo Wold, former White House Deputy Assistant for Domestic Policy under Trump, about the controversy surrounding Kroger’s move to offshore jobs.

Kroger, the largest traditional grocery chain in the nation, is facing strong blowback on social media over its plan to slash 3,000 jobs in the United States while advertising upcoming positions overseas in India.

In a recent development, the controversy comes as the Cincinnati-based grocer begins executing a three-year strategy it has previously announced to cut $5 billion in costs as part of a restructuring that will eliminate roughly 37% of its U.S. corporate workforce by 2029.

While Kroger maintains the reductions are aimed at lowering shelf prices through technology and leaner operations, simultaneous recruiting for a new hub in Bangalore has fueled online accusations that the organization is offshoring American jobs while asking shoppers to bear high food prices.

"‘They’re doing the jobs Americans don’t want to do,’" Theo Wold, a former White House deputy assistant for domestic policy during President Donald Trump's first term, posted on X. "No. They are taking jobs from Americans because it’s cheaper for corporations to hire foreigners.".

KEY AMERICAN INDUSTRY SEEING BLUE-COLLAR JOBS BOOM AS TRUMP'S RE-SHORING POLICIES PAY OFF.

A customer shops for eggs at a grocery store on March 12, 2025, in Chicago, Illinois. (Scott Olson/Getty Images).

In an interview with Fox News Digital, Wold said situations like this need to "start to be an honest conversation about penalizing businesses that take jobs and send them overseas.".

Rep. Nancy Mace (R-SC) responded on X by saying, "Hire American.".

"This insanity has to stop," retired Lt. Col. Buzz Patterson posted on X. "Reshore ALL US companies. We’re rapidly becoming India, and I didn’t serve 20 years defending that!".

FOOD DELIVERY FAVORITE FORCED TO FORK OVER MILLIONS AFTER DOJ ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION AGAINST AMERICAN WORKERS.

A Kroger grocery store in Covington, Kentucky, on Sunday, June 2, 2024. (Jeffrey Dean/Bloomberg via Getty Images).

"Kroger says these cuts are to ‘lower prices,’" workforce intelligence researcher Amanda Goodall wrote on X. "Classic. Do you think we will see lower prices at the grocery stores? I'm not holding my breath. I'm not a boycott person... but... damn. ".

In a statement, a Kroger spokesperson said the notifications "are part of the corporate headcount reduction the organization unveiled in early October to lower prices and improve the shopping experience by simplifying operations and better use of technology." Kroger declined to answer questions regarding how many U.S. roles are being shifted to its upcoming Bangalore capability center, the projected headcount in India or which departments were most affected.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP.

A young man shopping for groceries at the grocery store. (iStock).

It has been revealed that the first wave of layoff notices went out to corporate employees last week, marking the initial phase of an overhaul confirmed in October by CEO Greg Foran that will pare Kroger’s white-collar workforce from roughly 8,200 to 5,200. Frontline store and warehouse employees are not targeted by the cuts.

In an October internal memo announcing the 3,000-role reduction, Foran pointed to expanding artificial intelligence and workflow automation as a central driver for trimming corporate overhead.

At the same time, job boards have listed nearly 30 corporate openings for Kroger’s newly introduced Global Capability Center in Bangalore across finance, supply chain, real estate and data analytics. Chief Financial Officer David Kennerley previously told investors the overseas capability center would deliver modest savings in 2026 before generating more substantial cost reductions in 2027 and 2028.

Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter from Pasadena, California, who has been with Fox News Digital since 2021. You can reach him at AndrewMark.Miller@fox.com.

The Global Antiauthoritarian Wave Is an Illusion

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2707 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • BARTELS is University Distinguished Professor of Political Science and Law and May Werthan Shayne Chair of Public Policy and Social Science at Vanderbilt University.
  • In 2022, many observers celebrated the results of the United States’ midterm elections as a victory for democracy.
  • According to recent reports, but that rosy interpretation was more the result of wishful thinking than careful analysis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LARRY M. BARTELS is University Distinguished Professor of Political Science and Law and May Werthan Shayne Chair of Public Policy and Social Science at Vanderbilt University.

Democracy Can’t Be Saved at the Ballot Box.

In 2022, many observers celebrated the results of the United States’ midterm elections as a victory for democracy. The Republican Party underperformed at the ballot box, and some of the candidates most outspoken in support of former President Donald Trump’s historic effort to overturn the 2020 election outcome were among the casualties. President Joe Biden concluded that the American people “have proven once again that democracy is who we are.” New York Times reporters Nick Corasaniti, Reid Epstein, and Jonathan Weisman concurred, writing that the midterm outcome demonstrated “the resilience of the country’s democracy” as the electorate rejected “openly extremist Republican candidates.”.

According to recent reports, but that rosy interpretation was more the result of wishful thinking than careful analysis. Most of the Republicans who lost were simply bad, inexperienced candidates. In fact, Republican members of Congress who had flouted the democratic process by voting to decertify electoral votes on January 6, 2021, suffered no discernible penalty at the polls, while the minority who had stood up for the rule of law faced stiff backlash from their party’s establishment and from primary voters. And, of course, two years later, Trump stormed back into the White House.

In this year’s midterms, Trump’s party took another, even bigger beating. And again, there has been a rush to celebrate the result as a triumph for democratic values. NPR reported that “one of the major, clear winners of the midterms is American democracy itself.” Amanda Taub, an international affairs columnist at The Latest York Times, upped the ante, writing that “An anti-authoritarian wave appears to be crashing over elections around the world.” Just as in 2022, however, there is reason to fear that this optimistic account seriously misconstrues what happened at the polls on November 3 and what the result means for the future. History demonstrates that voters in the United States, as in other democracies, are much more focused on the competence of their political leaders and their own well-being than on adherence to democratic procedures. To imagine that they have suddenly become guardians of democratic norms is to misunderstand the electorate’s role in the democratic process—and to underestimate the chronic susceptibility of the American political system to democratic backsliding.

Sources indicate that it is natural to “feel pride,” as the Latest York Times editorial board put it, in the notion that ordinary citizens “stood up” for democratic principles at the ballot box. Democracy is the United States’ civil religion, and the voice of the people is the closest thing Americans have to the voice of God. But as the British jurist and historian Henry Sumner Maine observed in 1885, the oracle of democracy is often “not as intelligible as might be desired.” Electoral behavior is complex, and interpretations of election outcomes constructed in the hours and days after a vote often turn out to be far off the mark. Voters in democracies are less ideological than analysts generally assume. They are also less committed to abstract democratic norms than high-minded observers might hope. In a 2020 study, the Yale political scientists Matthew Graham and Milan Svolik used survey experiments to test the impact of democratic norm violations on Americans’ support for hypothetical candidates. They concluded that “only a small fraction of Americans prioritize democratic principles in their electoral choices when doing so goes against their partisan identification or favorite policies.” In 2022, real voters demonstrated the same point with their willingness to support Republican members of Congress who had participated in Trump’s bogus “stop the steal” effort.

It has been revealed that this year, the exit polls run by a consortium of American news organizations provided superficial support for the notion that the midterm “blue wave” was an explicit rejection of Trump’s continuing assault on democratic norms. These surveys asked voters which of six challenges was the most key facing the country. A third of respondents chose “the state of democracy,” and an overwhelming proportion of those who did, 79 percent, voted for Democratic congressional candidates. Taken at face value, these data suggest that more than a quarter of the electorate voted Democratic because they opposed Trump’s efforts to subvert American democracy.

It has been revealed that alas, people’s explanations for their own behavior are often misleading. Responses to list choices of this sort are particularly sensitive to the specific options presented and their favorable or unfavorable connotations. Given the choice, most people would probably prefer to attribute their votes to principled support for democracy than to pique at the price of gas. But when a separate YouGov poll conducted just after the vote asked an open-ended version of the same question, only five percent of voters spontaneously cited government corruption or the undermining of democracy as the most important factor motivating their choice.

A closer look at the exit poll data offers additional grounds for skepticism regarding the importance of democratic principles for the 2026 midterm outcome. The largest swing away from the Republican Party, more than 30 points, was among young voters—who are generally much less supportive of democracy than other age cohorts. (A 2025 Kettering Foundation survey, for instance, found that although 89 percent of Silent Generation respondents agreed with the proposition that “democracy is the best form of government,” only 54 percent of Gen Z respondents did.) To suppose that young people are now the vanguard of a sudden urge to defend democracy is implausible.

Sources indicate that finally, a comparison between the 2026 and 2024 exit polls is telling. In 2022, well before the depredations of Trump’s second term, voters were presented a similar list choice of issues that “mattered most in deciding how you voted for president.” A similar share of voters cited “the state of democracy” that year as did this year, and a similar overwhelming majority of them reported voting for Kamala Harris. The key difference between the two elections was not in the importance that voters assigned to democratic principles but in the impact of economic grievances. In 2024, 32 percent of exit poll respondents remarked the economy mattered most for their vote, and 81 percent of those respondents reported voting for Trump. In 2026, 39 percent said that the economy was the most important problem facing the country—and most of them voted for Democrats.

What about the notion that “an anti-authoritarian wave appears to be crashing over elections around the world”? As with many “waves” identified by political analysts, this antiauthoritarian trend mostly amounts to a short list of cases in which autocrats (or would-be autocrats) lost elections. Taub, the Newly introduced York Times commentator, pointed to Brazil, Hungary, and Serbia, along with the U.S. midterm elections, as evidence for a wave. But it is a stretch to see antiauthoritarian sentiment as the common thread explaining these outcomes.

Sources indicate that in Brazil in October, the incumbent president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (known as Lula), defeated Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of his right-wing populist predecessor, by less than four percentage points. The result was unremarkable, except for the fact that Bolsonaro had led Lula in the first round of voting. The most salient event separating the two votes was a televised debate in which Bolsonaro seemed to mock Lula for having lost a finger in a factory accident. “I was a minor and working at night,” Lula responded, “because either I worked or I did not eat. I will not accept a posh guy calling me ‘nine-fingers.’ ” It was a dramatic moment, but hardly a test of Brazilian voters’ commitment to democracy.

In a recent development, the April election in Hungary provides a clearer parallel with the U.S. midterm race. Viktor Orban’s Fidesz party was defeated after 16 years of autocratic rule—but Hungarians’ attitudes toward democracy likely played a smaller role in both Orban’s rise and his fall than many observers imagine. His triumph in 2010 was widely but erroneously portrayed as part of a global populist wave. In fact, data from the European Social Survey (ESS) show that his supporters were not more distrustful of politicians, more dissatisfied with democracy, more opposed to immigration or the EU, or more eager for order and tradition than other Hungarian voters. What they were, mostly, was fed up with their incumbent government.

In a recent development, orban used his sweeping election victory as a pretext to substantially erode Hungarian democracy, pressuring judges and the press and fiddling with election rules to entrench Fidesz’s dominance. Those moves no doubt contributed to his long tenure in office. But the more important factor was that, from 2009 to 2019, a series of ESS surveys recorded substantial increases in ordinary Hungarians’ satisfaction with their economy, their government, their lives as a whole, and, ironically, even “the way democracy works in Hungary.” When that sense of well-being faded, Orban’s autocratic machinations proved unable to protect him. As the Christian Science Monitor reporter Mark Sappenfield put it, “The story of his political demise is, in the end, not so different from countless democratic elections everywhere. The economy stagnated, highlighting levels of corruption that became intolerable to voters, who then lost trust in Mr. Orbán’s ability to guide them to better lives.”.

Much the same could be stated of Trump in 2026. One of the oldest and best-supported generalizations in political science is the law of the pendulum. It asserts that the political costs of governing—stemming from, for example, ideological overreach, complacency, scandals, or economic shocks—tend to erode support for incumbent political leaders and their parties, resulting in the restoration of competitive balance and periodic alteration of parties in power. Of course, these political costs do not accumulate with anything like the uniformity implied by the image of a pendulum swinging consistently from left to right and back again. Some governments are beset by problems and succumb in short order, while others face smoother seas and survive—for a time. But no democratic government lasts forever.

When incumbents use state resources—sometimes including legal and physical intimidation—to entrench themselves in power, it may feel like the law of the pendulum has been suspended. Nonetheless, even the most dominant political machines succumb eventually to hard times, economic and social change, internal divisions, and mounting pressure from those excluded from power. As the Vanderbilt political scientist Jessica Trounstine noted in a 2008 study of the rise and fall of political “bosses” in U.S. cities, the result may be chaotic: “In many cases the fall of monopolies set in motion periods of intense factionalism during which gridlock was common.” Turnover may result in protracted turmoil or in the emergence of a upcoming machine, perhaps under the banner of reform. The fall of a strongman or boss does not automatically produce a well-functioning democratic system.

Industry observers note that if characterizing the midterm elections as a triumph for democratic norms misconstrues why voters made their choices, it also risks misrepresenting what comes next. The New York Times editorial board envisioned quick progress to halt democratic backsliding: “The outcome creates a crucial check on Mr. Trump’s autocratic behavior. . . . The country already feels changed, and it will in fact be changed in January.”.

Changed, certainly; but the president and his allies are not going anywhere, and they are far from powerless. A glance around the world provides examples of the intense factionalism and gridlock that may be in store for the United States during the next two years. In Poland, an autocratic government fell in 2023 after eight years in power. But the holdover president, Karol Nawrocki, has battled Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s institutional reform efforts. Tusk’s attempt to remake the constitutional court—packed with friends of the former regime—precipitated a constitutional crisis pitting the prime minister and the EU against the president and mobs of right-wing protesters. Tusk’s election was just one step in what will be a long struggle to restore Poland’s liberal democracy.

Industry observers note that the American president is much more powerful than Poland’s, providing much more scope for bitter political conflict over policies and democratic procedures. In one election-night interview, Trump claimed that he would “look forward to working with” the victorious Democrats. But earlier in the day, to CBS News’s Robert Costa, he noted his victory in the Supreme Court case Trump v. Slaughter (which upheld his right to fire a Federal Trade Commission member) and claimed that “the Slaughter case gives the president tremendous powers that it never had before.” Another person Costa described as “close to the president” told him that “while Democrats may win” the election, the president would “keep the power to do almost everything he wants.” The post-election appointment of Stephen Miller as Trump’s chief of staff does not bode well for cooperation.

Of course, Democrats hope to win back the White House in 2028. But even if they do, it would be naive to expect Trump’s legacy of democratic backsliding to be erased. He has done substantial, durable harm to the federal government and the American political system. Some of his most egregious procedural and policy changes will be rolled back, but only by diverting attention and political capital from new priorities. Others will be harder to undo. Millions of years’ worth of governing experience cast aside in Elon Musk’s ham-handed purge of the civil service will not be restored with the stroke of a pen. The massive expansion of the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, its extensive network of detention facilities, and its culture—which the legal scholar L. Ali Khan described as “performative cruelty”—will not be swiftly or easily dismantled. The Supreme Court will not revert to the ideological mainstream any time soon.

Perhaps the most significant damage of the Trump era has been to long-standing, informal democratic norms that supposedly constrained the behavior of political leaders. Observers who expected Trump to pay a stiff political price for his abusive rhetoric, incessant lying, self-dealing, and disdain for court rulings, Congress, foreign allies, and the electoral process have learned that, as the University of Denver political scientist Seth Masket put it, “a lot of the things we think voters just won’t tolerate turn out to be tolerable to them.” That lesson, once learned, is very hard to unlearn. If future political leaders refrain from these behaviors, it will be because they want to, not because they think they have to.

According to recent reports, trump’s trashing of political norms accelerated a process that was already underway before he turned his sights on the White House. In 2012, the veteran political analysts Thomas Mann and Norman Ornstein argued that hyperpartisanship was eroding the compromise and self-restraint necessary to facilitate power sharing in the United States’ peculiarly decentralized national government. The logic of partisan tit for tat has encouraged each party to respond to the other’s norm violations by pushing even more aggressively to weaponize the filibuster, bypass Congress with executive orders, and gerrymander congressional district boundaries. Each successful norm violation has encouraged further probing of legal and political redlines.

Hyperpartisanship will not disappear when Trump departs the political scene; he is its consequence more than its cause. Most important, the passion that has fueled the Make America Great Again movement will not vanish. Millions of Americans still see the waves of social change that have washed over the United States since the 1960s as a cultural disaster, and the looming prospect of a majority-minority country as a threat to be battled, by undemocratic means if necessary. They will find upcoming champions.

A survey commissioned by NPR and PBS to mark the United States’ 250th birthday found that 82 percent of Americans agreed that “the issues that divide the nation” constitute “a serious threat to the future of our democracy.” If that seems alarmist, it is worth noting that 37 percent of the same respondents in the same survey—and 58 percent of those under the age of 30—agreed that “Americans may have to resort to violence in order to get the country back on track.” When people view political conflict in existential terms, they are unlikely to feel constrained by high-minded democratic theory.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that catalonia’s independence movement is moving to the right, and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez might pay the price in snap parliamentary elections on Nov. 29. Junts per Catalunya, the separatist party that supported Sánchez to form a minority government in 2023, turned against him last year to fend off a latest far-right rival—ultimately forcing the early vote.

Recent findings suggest that sánchez called elections after failing to get emergency legislation aimed at tackling Spain’s housing crisis through parliament in October. The conservative People’s Party (PP), the far-right Vox party, and the center-right Junts all voted against the package.

Catalonia’s independence movement is moving to the right, and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez might pay the price in snap parliamentary elections on Nov. 29. Junts per Catalunya, the separatist party that supported Sánchez to form a minority government in 2023, turned against him last year to fend off a fresh far-right rival—ultimately forcing the early vote.

Sánchez called elections after failing to get emergency legislation aimed at tackling Spain’s housing crisis through parliament in October. The conservative People’s Party (PP), the far-right Vox party, and the center-right Junts all voted against the package.

According to recent reports, it was the latest example of Junts going against the minority government’s initiatives. When party head Carles Puigdemont revealed that Junts would revoke its backing and move into the opposition last year, he blamed Sánchez’s Socialist Workers’ Party for broken promises. But the pro-independence party is also facing a growing threat at home in Catalonia.

That threat is Aliança Catalana—a far-right, separatist party led by Sílvia Orriols, the mayor of the small town of Ripoll. Orriols founded Aliança in 2020 after breaking with another separatist party; its platform combines a demand for Catalan independence with hard-line hostility toward immigration and Islam. She pushed for a tougher approach to immigration after the 2017 Barcelona attacks, carried out by a terror cell based in Ripoll.

It has been revealed that unlike Junts, Aliança has elected not to stand in the Nov. 29 national elections, refusing to take part based on its Catalonian separatism. “We are not thinking about influencing Madrid, and that’s part of the foundation of Aliança,” remarked the party’s press chief, Eduard Berraondo.

Polling presently points to a right-wing majority. The PP leads with 31.2 percent of the vote, with the Socialists at 29.3 percent, and Vox at 18 percent as of Nov. 24, according to newspaper Ara’s polling average. Together, the PP and Vox are projected to win around 190 seats, above the 176 needed for a majority in the 350-seat Congress of Deputies. Only the state-run Center for Sociological Studies pollster, which critics say favors the government, puts the Socialists ahead.

So, although Aliança isn’t on the ballot, its rapid rise is reshaping Spanish politics.

Sources indicate that the party’s hard line on immigration and Islam has pushed Junts to the right, making the party ever less likely to partner with the Socialists. Aliança’s voters could help decide where Catalonia’s right-wing vote goes: back to Junts, across to Vox, or nowhere at all. Finally, the party’s growing popularity suggests a deeper shift among Catalan independence supporters, away from progressivism and toward a more exclusionary view of who counts as Catalan.

Aliança has risen rapidly in Catalonia. The far-right party won just two of 135 seats in the Catalan parliamentary elections in 2024, but the latest survey from the Catalan government’s polling agency, the Centre d’Estudis d’Opinió (CEO), projects that the party would capture between 23 and 25 seats if regional elections were held now. Junts, which holds 35 seats, would fall to between 18 and 20.

Industry observers note that catalonia’s next regional elections must be held by late June 2028. Almost 1 in 5 people who voted for Junts in 2024 now say they would back Aliança—but a majority of those wavering respondents still ranked Junts as their second choice.

Aliança’s message lands with voters anxious about rapid population growth, crime, and stretched public services. Around 18 percent of its supporters say they would vote for Vox on Nov. 29, according to the CEO. This matters in Madrid, where each seat that Junts loses weakens the leverage that once made it a kingmaker.

Junts is responding to Aliança’s rise by shifting to the right. The party has demanded that Madrid hand Catalonia control over immigration, backed bans on the burqa and niqab in public spaces, and pushed for tougher rules on repeat criminal offenders. The party has also proposed making immigrants wait 10 years after registering as residents before they can apply for subsidized housing, more than three times the current maximum.

Catalonia elects 48 members of Spain’s national parliament; Junts holds seven of those seats. In return for the party’s support after the 2023 election, the Socialists pushed through an amnesty law covering those involved in the 2017 Catalan independence push, including Puigdemont, who at the time served as Catalonia’s president and fled to Belgium to avoid arrest. The Supreme Court lifted his arrest warrant in October, clearing the way for his return.

In a recent development, junts has ruled out backing either Sánchez or the PP’s party leader for prime minister, though it has left the door open to supporting a different Socialist candidate. Competing with Aliança for allegiance in Catalonia, it has little room to prop up a left-wing government. With a PP-Vox majority, that might not matter. But if the right-wing vote falls short, Spain’s government could once again hang on a handful of Catalan votes.

Industry observers note that the CEO expects Junts to win just four or five parliamentary seats in the snap elections, while Vox could more than double its share of Catalonia’s seats—from two seats to five or six. Some of those votes might come from Aliança supporters.

In a recent development, “From Nov. 29, a dual voter will emerge: someone who votes Aliança in municipal and Catalan elections, and Vox in Spanish ones,” mentioned Xavier Torrens, a professor of political science at the University of Barcelona.

Vox and Aliança are opposed when it comes to the question of Catalonia’s independence, but on immigration, they speak the same language.

“Many people vote Vox because they reject immigration, feel unsafe, or believe immigrants take a large share of public benefits. Aliança says the same,” mentioned Xavier Rius, a Catalan journalist and the author of a book on Aliança.

Berraondo rejected a direct comparison between his party and Vox, insisting that their positions overlap only on immigration and law and order and that Aliança does not share Vox’s opposition to abortion and gay rights.

Still, Aliança might see a PP-Vox victory as good news for its future. “Imagine you think that if the PP and Vox win the elections in November, they could start the dirty job of changing the immigration rules,” Berraondo stated. “Then you can take advantage of it if you are in government in Catalonia in 2028.”.

This political convergence would once have been unthinkable. The Catalan independence movement defined itself against the Spanish nationalism that Vox represents and long prided itself on being progressive, inclusive, and pro-European. Center-right parties joined the independence push in the 2010s, but Aliança is the first far-right separatist party to gain traction in Catalonia.

So, how did a far-right party emerge from the movement, and why now? Part of the answer lies in 2017. That October, Catalonia’s pro-independence government held a referendum that Spain’s Constitutional Court had declared illegal. Puigdemont signed a declaration of independence and then days later declared that he asked parliament to suspended it. Weeks later, Madrid suspended Catalonia’s autonomy, and the movement’s leaders were jailed or fled abroad.

For many Junts supporters, the promise that independence was within reach proved hollow. Puigdemont’s about-face and rush to negotiate with Madrid seemed to reveal that the party prioritized its political leverage over independence—a perception later reinforced when Junts backed Sanchez’s government and demanded amnesty for its leaders rather than any move toward independence.

It has been revealed that orriols, the Aliança leader, has built her appeal on that sense of betrayal, casting the referendum moment as a deception and Puigdemont as a leader who lost his nerve. Voters who have switched allegiance from Junts to Aliança are, on average, around 56 years old, with nearly 89 percent supporting independence, according to the CEO. Their top concerns are immigration and insecurity. These are disappointed separatists—not newcomers to the cause.

“Part of Junts’s electorate realized that the whole narrative about independence was just fluff, that they weren’t serious about it,” mentioned Massimo Maoret, a professor at IESE Business School in Barcelona and a longtime observer of Catalan politics. Aliança, he added, has tapped into that feeling “together with anti-immigrant, and especially anti-Islamic, sentiment.”.

According to recent reports, further, as the cost of living rises, the concerns over affordable housing that brought down Sánchez’s government have also boosted the far-right party. Aliança “is winning an anti-system, anti-establishment vote, driven by people being fed up with the rising cost of living, the high cost of housing, and the poor functioning of public services such as rail transport,” Torrens said.

According to recent reports, aliança has drawn a connection between those concerns and immigration, from pushing a debate over who counts as Catalan. For decades, the independence movement embraced a slogan popularized by Jordi Pujol, a former Catalan president: “Anyone who lives and works in Catalonia is Catalan.”.

Aliança takes a different line. “Aliança considers that only some of Catalonia’s inhabitants are Catalan, while the rest are immigrants settled in Catalonia but not Catalan,” Torrens stated. Orriols has said that Muslims could not be Catalan because “they don’t integrate with the country’s culture and values.”.

Why Spain’s Sánchez has succeeded while Britain’s Starmer floundered.

The question is the extent to which Aliança is shaping the independence movement. Junts has already shifted toward some of Aliança’s positions on immigration—but Jordi Turull, Junts’s secretary-general, has warned that the far right “will do nothing but take us further from our goal of a prosperous and complete Catalan republic.”.

In a recent development, josep Vila, the president of the Catalan National Assembly, a grassroots pro-independence organization, declined to say whether Aliança belonged to the movement. The group was “not concerned by the diversity of political options,” Vila wrote in an email, as long as they shared a strategy for independence.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, Aliança’s base is broadening beyond the independence movement. According to the CEO, only 53 percent of its supporters now back independence, down from 62 percent late last year. Taken together, the data suggest a shift in priorities. For disillusioned separatists and newcomers alike, concerns about immigration, security, and the cost of living increasingly outweigh the question of independence.

According to recent reports, in some ways, Catalonia seems to be following a familiar European script of an emergent far right—this time from within a separatist movement. Torrens makes a distinction between national-populist parties that took decades to break through, such as France’s National Rally, and those that do so within a few years, such as Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy, Portugal’s Chega, and Vox itself.

In a recent development, aliança, he said, is on the fast track. The party’s first test comes in this week’s snap elections, when its supporters could shape the outcome. The bigger tests come later: municipal elections in May 2027 and the regional election by 2028. For now, Aliança seems to have shifted the Catalan independence movement’s center of gravity, as a movement that prided itself on building a Catalonia for all has absorbed an us-versus-them view of who belongs.

Industry observers note that the Nov. 29 vote will offer the first signs of how far that shift reaches beyond Catalonia. If Junts loses seats in Madrid, and especially if the PP and Vox win a majority on their own, then Catalan separatists could lose their leverage over Spain’s government for the first time in years. The irony is that some of Aliança’s own supporters might help sweep the nationalists in.

Recent findings suggest that ES Foundry, a U.S. manufacturer of high-efficiency solar cells, is at RE+ 2026 this week to showcase its American-made solar cells and announce a milestone in its operating capacity.

According to the firm, it is the first and only crystalline silicon solar cell manufacturer to ship more than 1 gigawatt (GW) of domestically manufactured solar cells in the United States.

As one of the few U.S. solar cell manufacturers with a fully operational facility producing and shipping cells to customers, ES Foundry is helping move American solar manufacturing to commercial reality.

Industry observers note that in July, the organization unveiled it reached its full 3-GW manufacturing capacity. The company began production on its first 1-GW line last year and has now completed its 2-GW expansion line.

Solar Power World attended the opening of its Greenwood, South Carolina facility last year, reporting on its manufacturing outfit and its unique approach to supply deals that include working with large-scale project developers and utilities to guarantee domestic content supplies.

In a recent development, at RE+, attendees can see its U.S.-manufactured high-efficiency monocrystalline bifacial PERC solar cells and meet with manufacturer representatives to discuss domestic sourcing, manufacturing capabilities, and the evolving needs of the U.S. solar market.

“There’s an crucial difference between talking about building a domestic solar supply chain and actually making it happen,” stated ES Foundry CEO Alex Zhu in a statement. “At ES Foundry, we’re manufacturing at commercial scale, shipping cells to customers and navigating the realities of U.S. production every day. That experience gives us a unique perspective on what it will take to build a competitive, sustainable American solar industry. Success requires more than manufacturing capacity. It requires the right economics, technology investments, customer demand and policies to support long-term growth. We’re proud to be delivering on the promise of American manufacturing today while helping shape the industry’s future.”.

Visit ES Foundry at RE+ 2026: Booth C7434, November 16–19, Las Vegas, Nevada.

According to recent reports, rep.-elect LaKesha Womack, D-N.C., poses for a portrait after Congressional freshmen of the 120th Congress participated in a group photograph on the steps of the House of Representatives at the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 12, 2026, in Washington, D.C. — just two days after appearing in court on a felony summons and just days before paying the settlement for an unreturned rental car. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images).

Nearly two weeks after she was declared the winner in the Nov. 3 election, flipping a Republican-held seat, a North Carolina Democrat settled a 2019 rental car bill for a car she did not return, allowing prosecutors to drop a felony charge.

Mecklenburg County District Attorney Spencer B. Merriweather III, a fellow Democrat, dropped the case that featured a court summons served to Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack, D-N.C., at a campaign event Oct. 11, more than six years after the Jan. 14, 2020 summons was secured by prosecutors.

According to recent reports, womack said she did not know she was wanted for a felony because she was homeless at the time and not able to receive mail. She paid off the rental car organization as part of an agreement last week.

DEMOCRAT WHO TOPPLED GOP INCUMBENT WILL HEAD TO COURT ON FELONY CHARGE JUST DAYS AFTER ELECTION UPSET.

Recent findings suggest that rep.-elect LaKesha Womack, D-N.C., used her battle with diabetes, a hospital stay, single motherhood and homelessness in her campaign to flip a Republican House seat in the once-red state of North Carolina. (LaKesha Womack Facebook).

Sources indicate that "On November 16, 2026, this office was informed of an agreement reached between Defendant Womack and the rental dealer," Merriweather's DA office wrote in a statement Tuesday. "In the days that followed, we were able to confirm that the victim rental corporation received a sum of money from the Defendant equal to an assessed rental cost from the day the vehicle was deemed overdue until the day it came back into the possession of the victim corporation.

"In a subsequent phone call with a prosecutor, representatives for the victim rental corporation mentioned explicitly that the corporation did not wish to proceed further with prosecution and considered the matter resolved.".

Recent findings suggest that womack first appeared in court on the summons one week after being declared a future U.S. House member, and nearly seven years after the summons was issued. The rental car agreement was from Oct. 11, 2019, according to the district attorney, and the car was seized by local law enforcement on Dec. 4, 2019.

Womack said she did not receive the official felony court summons until Oct. 11, 2026 — less than a month before the midterm elections — when an officer personally handed her the paperwork at a campaign event.

DEMOCRAT HOUSE CANDIDATE HIT WITH FELONY SUMMONS AT CAMPAIGN EVENT.

Recent findings suggest that rep.-elect LaKesha Womack, D-N.C., went from Election Day to a felony court summons a week earlier this month and now heads to her swearing in to Congress in early January. (Getty Images).

Womack has spoken publicly about being homeless without a permanent mailing address after moving back to Charlotte in 2016 to work on the Hillary Clinton campaign.

In a recent development, "I was struggling," she said in an October video posted to Facebook. "I was struggled so bad that there were days that I wanted to end my life – that I did not think I was strong enough to push forward.

In a recent development, "At one point, I had a rental car, and I did not return the rental car on time. I did not know that they had filed a case against me, because, again, I was homeless and I had no place to receive mail, so I didn't get any notification about it.".

She added she was "going to figure out how much money do y'all need" to settle. That happened after her first court appearance, according to the district attorney's office's news release.

Fox News Digital reached out to Womack's campaign for comment, but they did not immediately respond.

STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE.

In a recent development, rep. Tim Moore, R-N.C., was just a one-term House member, having served in the North Carolina State House from 2003 to 2025, including five terms as state House speaker from 2015. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images).

It has been revealed that just a week prior, Womack defeated incumbent Rep. Tim Moore, R-N.C., by roughly two points in the race to represent North Carolina’s 14th Congressional District. She had rebuked campaign attack ads from friends of Moore targeting her late in the race, calling "the timing of my court date (one full week after Election Day) especially frustrating" and saying diabetes, an intensive car visit, single motherhood and homelessness contributed to her delinquency.

Recent findings suggest that "I have experienced some incredibly difficult chapters in my life, including a serious medical emergency that required hospitalization in intensive care," Womack told WBTV-3 just days before the election. "As a single mother living with type 1 Diabetes, that experience was frightening, overwhelming and life-changing. Like millions of Americans, I learned firsthand how rapidly an unexpected medical crisis can disrupt your health, financial stability, and ability to provide for your family.".

The charge, felony failure to return hired property, stemmed from a 2019 Toyota Corolla with an estimated value of $20,000 that Womack rented from Budget Car Rental on Aug. 27, 2019, according to prosecutors and court records. Womack renewed the agreement twice, with the final rental period beginning Oct. 7, 2019, before local law enforcement recovered the vehicle and returned it to the tech giant Dec. 4, 2019.

Recent findings suggest that womack’s attorney, Harold Cogdell Jr., told NBC News in a statement Tuesday that his client had been "unaware a criminal summons had issued" for nearly seven years and moved rapidly to settle the balance once notified. Cogdell noted that the Corolla was returned undamaged 41 days before the criminal charge was filed.

AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI.

The felony became a central attack line in the closing stretch of the race, with Republican ads warning voters against electing a "felony defendant.".

Industry observers note that president Donald Trump addresses the FAA ground stop and broader technology disruptions, calling the nation’s air traffic control system outdated. Responding to Fox News' Aishah Hasnie, Trump indicates air travel remains safe and outlines his request for $50 billion from the Senate to upgrade the system.

Criticism is mounting among experts concerned with the U.S. Army's "risky" plan to resume helicopter training flights near Washington National Airport following a deadly midair collision in 2025.

Sources indicate that the Army released a initiative and told select members of Congress it wants to restart helicopter test flights near DCA — just a few miles from the Pentagon — as soon as Dec. 1, 2026. Backlash immediately ensued.

Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., asserted on X he has "grave concerns about the decision to resume training flights before the NTSB’s safety recommendations have been fully implemented.".

A spokesperson for the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) told Fox News Digital that it "has not received a formal request to resume military helicopter flights around Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA).".

"Approval from the agency is required before any training in the area can restart," the spokesperson added.

FAA, NTSB INVESTIGATING POSSIBLE VIOLATION OF SAFETY PROTOCOL INVOLVING TRUMP, MARINE ONE.

Rep. Don Beyer Jr., D-Va., attends a protest in Washington. (Tom Williams/Getty Images).

A U.S. Army Black Hawk helicopter collided with American Airlines Flight 5342 in January 2025, killing all 67 people aboard both aircrafts. The FAA subsequently halted military helicopter training flights in the area in May 2025 after another Black Hawk helicopter flew too close to DCA, forcing air traffic controllers to reroute some commercial flights.

In a March 14, 2025, statement the FAA mentioned it was "permanently closing [helicopter] Route 4 between Hains Point and the Wilson Bridge and evaluating alternative helicopter routes as recommended by the NTSB.".

Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., on Monday wrote in an X post that the Army told his office it had reached out to the FAA regarding its request to resume training flights and is presently "awaiting a response.".

"Army officials assured my office that no flights will take place unless they are approved by the FAA," Beyer stated.

His office did not expand on specific concerns when reached by Fox News Digital on Tuesday.

An anonymous Army spokesperson told Politico on Monday "there is intent to resume flights," acknowledging that the move would require approval from the FAA.

TRUMP HELICOPTER’S RADIO WARNINGS WENT UNHEARD BEFORE CLOSE CALL WITH PASSENGER JET, REPORT CLAIMS.

A piece of wreckage is lifted from the water onto a salvage vessel near the site in the Potomac River of a midair collision between an American Airlines jet and a Black Hawk helicopter, at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, Feb. 4, 2025, in Arlington, Virginia. (AP).

The DOT referred Fox News Digital to the FAA when reached for comment.

"Members of the investigative team and I were briefed on the Army’s plans to begin the initial phase of a return to helicopter flights to the Pentagon through airspace near DCA as soon as December 1st," NTSB Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy told Fox News Digital.

It has been revealed that "It is our understanding that the FAA has yet to receive a formal request for these flights. We have not seen the Army’s concept of operations and look forward to reviewing it once it is formally submitted to the FAA for evaluation.".

FAA UNVEILS NEWLY INTRODUCED AIR TRAFFIC CONTROLLER HIRING PROPOSAL AFTER CHIEF WARNED SYSTEM WAS ‘CHRONICALLY UNDERSTAFFED’.

Sources indicate that when reached for comment on Tuesday, the Department of War referred Fox News Digital to the Army. The Army did not respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

Resuming helicopter training flights near DCA could pose "major" safety concerns, according to Randy Klatt, flight safety officer at the Foundation for Aviation Safety (FAS).

Industry observers note that "Yes, [there are] major concerns considering that no entity — the airlines, DCA, FAA, or the Army — took any proactive action on the thousands of loss-of-separation incidents that preceded the midair collision. Helicopter Route 4 was a trap as designed, yet it was in use regularly until disaster struck," Klatt told Fox News Digital on Tuesday. "Knowing this does not instill any confidence that the resumption of Army training flights will be done safely and in close coordination with the FAA.".

"There has been no mention of reopening Helicopter Route 4 but for the above reasons FAS would strongly oppose such an action," he added.

Sources indicate that the air traffic control tower after the American Airlines crash at the Reagan National Airport on Feb. 3, 2025, in Arlington, Virginia. (Kayla Bartkowski/Getty Images).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that as solar and energy storage portfolios grow in both size and complexity, managing performance is just one part of the equation. Owners and operators must also keep track of power purchase agreements (PPAs), warranties, service contracts, billing, compliance requirements and project-level profitability.

It has been revealed that enSights is looking to bring those responsibilities together with the launch of its AI Studio, a latest addition to its Energy Business Management (EBM) platform. The company declared the launch Nov. 10.

In a recent development, the AI Studio is designed to give solar and storage owners, operators, and asset managers access to a customizable team of AI specialists that can support business and operational workflows. Through no-code tools, customers can create AI dashboards and reports using natural-language instructions, while still establishing their own workflows, routines, data-access permissions and approval requirements.

The approach here reflects a broader shift toward renewable energy software, it’s moving beyond monitoring individual assets toward managing the financial and operational performance of entire portfolios.

It has been revealed that according to enSights, its EBM platform brings together energy management systems (EMS), production data, billing, PPA information, operations and maintenance, contractual obligations and compliance on a unified data foundation. That integration is central to the tech giant’s AI strategy.

Rather than limiting AI applications to identifying equipment complications or answering generation-related questions, the platform is designed to connect energy production with the contracts and financial obligations associated with each project.

In a recent development, the AI Studio includes an orchestrator that coordinates specialized AI agents focused on areas like monitoring, operations, revenue, warranties, permits, lenders, insurers, and asset management. For portfolio managers, those capabilities could help reduce the time spent reviewing disconnected systems and manually reconciling information across departments. Automated reviews of contractual obligations, revenue performance and operational alerts could also help teams identify issues earlier and direct attention to matters that still require human intervention.

The enSights AI Studio dashboard provides solar and energy storage operators with AI-powered tools for asset management, operational workflows, and financial oversight. Credit: enSights.

Recent findings suggest that enSights emphasized that people remain in control of the AI Team. Customers determine which workflows the agents handle and where approvals are required. Physical asset controls remain governed by established EMS and site-level systems.

The AI Studio also builds on an expanded financial management offering within the EBM platform. Its Financial Asset Management Module includes revenue assurance, contract, and obligation management, and profit-and-loss reporting.

The module is intended to provide project-level financial visibility, helping companies identify and prevent revenue losses while generating reports for investors.

The platform also includes real-time EMS, weather and tariff forecasting, along with dispatch planning intended to optimize revenue while maintaining grid safety and local compliance.

It has been revealed that enSights indicates its platform is deployed globally across more than 100,000 sites, representing over 5 GW of assets. The firm prepares to demonstrate the AI Studio and its broader EBM platform at RE+ 2026.

As AI gains traction across the clean energy industry, the next competitive advantage could come from connecting operational intelligence with the financial and contractual decisions that determine how successfully renewable energy portfolios perform.
